s: The two clauses can pull against each other: accommodating religion may look like favoring it.

The Court recognizes "play in the joints," a space where government may accommodate religion without being required to (Walz; Locke v. Davey, 2004, allowing exclusion of devotional theology degrees from scholarships, a holding later narrowed).

Accommodations are permissible when they lift government-imposed burdens on religion and do not impose significant burdens on third parties (Corporation of Presiding Bishop v. Amos, 1987, Title VII exemption for religious employers; Cutter v. Wilkinson, 2005, RLUIPA).
An accommodation that absolutely privileges religious interests over all others crosses the line (Estate of Thornton v. Caldor, 1985).
Religious institutions enjoy autonomy in matters of faith, doctrine and internal governance, including selecting ministers.
Disputes over church property must be resolved under neutral principles of law, without deciding doctrinal questions (Jones v. Wolf, 1979).
